title: Chen-An (Evan) Pai
text:
I am a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia. I came here from computer science at National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan, where I spent most of my degree on the systems side of machine learning — making large models run faster on GPU clusters, and teaching other students how to do the same.
That work took me to three international student cluster competitions. My teams placed 3rd at SC24 in Atlanta, 2nd at ISC 2024 in Hamburg, and 1st at the 2023 APAC HPC-AI Competition, on problems ranging from MLPerf Stable Diffusion benchmarking to an 11.4× speedup on BLOOM inference. Somewhere in the middle of optimizing other people’s models, I got curious about the models themselves — and about how much of a reported result is real.
MDS is the other half of that education. I already know how to make a model run; I came here to learn how to tell whether it should be trusted. I am looking for machine learning engineer and data scientist roles where both halves matter.
More detail is on the about page, my work is on projects, and I write about the program on the blog.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation week was mostly logistics — accounts, laptops, a room full of people introducing themselves — but the part that stuck with me was how quickly the cohort stopped being strangers. Everyone had arrived from somewhere different: economics, biology, public health, a few people coming back after years of work. I had half expected a room of computer science graduates like me, and instead spent the week being reminded that most of the interesting questions in this field arrive from somewhere other than the code.
Then classes started, and the pace was the real surprise. I knew MDS was compressed; I had not internalised what a block schedule feels like from the inside. A topic is introduced, you use it in a lab two days later, and by the following week it is assumed knowledge. Coming from a background where I would spend a week profiling a single application before changing anything, the instinct to understand a thing completely before starting stopped working almost immediately. What replaced it was starting before I felt ready and letting the gaps show up in the error messages.
A few weeks in, I have settled somewhere between overwhelmed and genuinely enjoying it. The tooling has been the easiest part to love — Git and the shell I already knew from cluster work, and Quarto has quietly replaced a pile of habits I did not realise were slowing me down; this site is a direct result. The statistics is where I am working hardest, and that is exactly why I came. I spent my undergraduate years making models run faster without being able to say much about whether their results deserved the compute. That is the gap I am here to close. Ask me again after the first round of quizzes.



Vancouver from campus during my first week at UBC.

title: Projects
text: A few things explained properly, rather than a long list. Most of this work was done on GPU clusters, either for international student cluster competitions or as research and internship work.

title: Projects
section: Local LLM deployment and inference optimization
text:
Local LLM deployment and inference optimization
The problem. Running a 70-billion-parameter model as an interactive chatbot is a throughput problem, not a modelling one. Naive serving leaves most of the GPU idle between requests.
What I did. Built an end-to-end local chatbot around LLaMA 3.1 70B, served with vLLM behind a Gradio front end on 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, then worked through the inference path — continuous batching, kernel-level tuning, and memory layout.
Outcome. 3× throughput increase over the baseline deployment, with the whole system running locally rather than against a hosted API.
LLaMA 3.1 · vLLM · Gradio · CUDA · 4× H100

title: Projects
text:
SC24 Student Cluster Competition — 3rd place
Atlanta, US · November 2024 · the leading global HPC-AI student competition
Three tasks over four days, on a cluster we configured and tuned ourselves:

MLPerf benchmarking. Optimized Stable Diffusion for MLPerf on 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs using TensorRT, tuning precision and kernel selection against the benchmark’s accuracy constraints.
Mystery application — cat object detection. Trained YOLO11x for a same-day object detection challenge, placing 3rd in that task.
Reproducibility challenge. Reproduced the findings of the DataLife paper on the 1000 Genomes Project — the task that did the most to convince me I wanted the statistical half of this education.

The reproducibility work became a peer-reviewed critique, now in press at IEEE TPDS (DOI: 10.1109/TPDS.2025.3627428).
TensorRT · Stable Diffusion · YOLO11x · MLPerf · reproducibility

title: Projects
text:
ISC High Performance SCC 2024 — 2nd place
Hamburg, Germany · May 2024 · one of the top three global supercomputing competitions
The problem. Take Neko, a spectral-element CFD application, and make it run as fast as possible on a 10 × NVIDIA H100 cluster within a fixed power budget.
What I did. Profiled the solver to find where the time actually went, then worked on parallel decomposition, communication patterns, and system-level tuning rather than guessing at compiler flags.
Outcome. 18.5× speedup over the starting configuration, and 2nd place overall.
CFD · parallel programming · MPI/NCCL · profiling · 10× H100

title: Projects
text:
APAC HPC-AI Competition 2023 — 1st place
Sydney, Australia · February 2024 · against 21 teams from 17 universities
The problem. Optimize inference for the BLOOM large language model across a multi-GPU cluster.
What I did. Combined tensor parallelism, DeepSpeed inference optimization, and NVIDIA NCCL collective tuning, measuring each change instead of stacking them and hoping.
Outcome. 11.4× inference speedup, and first place overall.
BLOOM · tensor parallelism · DeepSpeed · NCCL · LLM inference

title: Projects
text:
FourCastNet end-to-end deployment — 2nd place
High Performance Application Competition 2023 · Hsinchu, Taiwan · against 8 teams from 7 universities
Deployed and ran FourCastNet, an AI-driven global climate model, end to end: environment setup, multi-node training, inference, and visualization. Less a single-technique problem than a test of whether you can carry a full AI workflow from a bare cluster to a finished result.
FourCastNet · multi-node training · full-stack AI workflow

Quantum machine learning classifier
National Center for High-performance Computing · Hsinchu, Taiwan · Summer 2023
Implemented a data re-uploading classifier using quantum machine learning methods in PennyLane, as part of a summer software engineering internship at NCHC.
PennyLane · QML · research

title: About
text:
I grew up and studied in Taiwan, and finished a Bachelor of Computer Science at National Tsing Hua University in July 2025, graduating with a 3.97 GPA and ranked 43rd of 183 in my class.
My degree pulled me steadily toward the systems end of machine learning. Between 2023 and 2025 I was a teaching assistant for four NTHU courses — Operating Systems, Parallel Programming, and both the fundamental and advanced High Performance Computing Cluster Practice courses — which meant two years of explaining schedulers, MPI, and GPU clusters to people who had not seen them before. Teaching a thing is still the fastest way I know to find out whether I actually understand it.
Alongside that I interned as a Data Scientist at IBM in Taipei and as a Software Engineer at the National Center for High-performance Computing, where I built a data re-uploading classifier using quantum machine learning methods in PennyLane.

title: About
text:
Why data science
Most of my work has been on the engineering side of a model: how fast it runs, how many GPUs it needs, how to squeeze another 3× out of the inference path. That is satisfying, and it is only half the problem.
The other half kept showing up as a question I could not answer properly. A benchmark improves — is the improvement real, or an artifact of how it was measured? A model reports an accuracy — would it hold on next month’s data? During the SC24 Reproducibility Challenge my team reproduced the findings of the DataLife paper on the 1000 Genomes Project, and that experience made the gap obvious: I had strong intuitions about systems and weak ones about evidence.
MDS is me closing that gap deliberately — statistics, inference, and experiment design, taught properly rather than picked up in passing.
